translation:
According to the teaching of Kabirji and Jivanji, what should the true nature of bhakti (devotion) be? This is a very important question. In the previous chapter Jivanji Maharaj explained that studying the Vedas, the scriptures and the Puranas, and observing celibacy (brahmacharya) — even after doing all this a person does not attain the supreme state (param gati). Beyond this, wearing the tilak mark and the tulsi necklace, singing the praises taught in the Vedas, going on pilgrimage, keeping vows, performing yajna, japa (repetition of the divine name), giving charity, offering arghya (ceremonial water offering), and daily recitation (adhyapan, the regular reading of scripture) — all of these are karmas (actions) by which a person becomes bound again and again. Liberation is not obtained through these actions; these are merely the mistaken practices taught by the six schools of philosophy (shat darshan shastras). Cessation of action is itself the supreme state. Then how can cessation be attained by performing more actions? It is for this very reason that Adhyaruji Maharaj says—

_van hari bhakti ajanave, na kahe koi taharo maram_
_krut karma bhogave ek game, biji game sache karam ||4||_
_evade sankashta sankalu, kane uvekhu tat_
_karma tane shir sompine, shastre muki vat ||5||_
_juna bhogavi nigame, nava tano kare parihar_
_eni pare nishkarma jo hoy, to havada hoy par ||6||_
_jaha lagi ek karam hoy, taha na chhute avatar_
_bhogavava deh dharave, sahe jamna bahu mar ||7||_
_deh dhare nishkarmapanu nathi, pan na mahelu hari nam_
_pames nam sharan vade, nishkarmapanu nirvan ||8||_
(One who is unacquainted with devotion to Hari — no one can tell of your secret. He goes on undergoing the actions he has done, whether they please him or not; that alone is true action. Such distress is a heavy chain — why neglect it, dear one? Having placed the burden of karma on its own head, the scriptures have simply left the matter there. If one exhausts old actions by undergoing them and gives up new ones, and thus becomes free of action, then even now one crosses over. As long as a single karma remains, the soul is not released from taking birth; it must take a body to undergo it, and suffer greatly at the hands of Yama's messengers. Simply taking a body does not by itself bring freedom from action, but through taking refuge in Hari's Name it does; freedom from action, the state of nirvana, is attained through the refuge of the Name.) — (Kadvu 3, verses 5–8)

Whoever is unacquainted with devotion to Shri Hari, and moreover does not know the inner secret (marma) of the Supreme Brahman, such a soul (jivatma) goes on undergoing one action after another in this world. Whether the action is good or not good, he must still undergo it. And this process is like ghee poured on fire — just as fire blazes up more and more fiercely when ghee is poured on it, and such a fire is never extinguished, so the soul remains caught in distress in just this way. Because such souls place blind faith in the scriptures, they become more and more miserable. The rule that applies to ordinary human beings does not apply to devotees (bhaktas). Taking a body and undergoing action does not by itself bring freedom from action; freedom from action can be attained only through taking refuge in the divine Name. Without devotion, though, one must indeed go on undergoing the fruits of action.

_avashyameva bhoktavyam kritam karma shubhashubham_
_na abhuktam na kshiyate karma kalpa koti shatairapi_
(Good or bad action once performed must certainly be undergone; it does not wear away even over hundreds of millions of kalpas without being experienced.)

Whatever action must be undergone will certainly have to be undergone, for without being undergone it does not wear away even over crores of kalpas.

Sadguru Jivanji Maharaj says—

_lakhya mite nahi jivana, jo kachhu lakhiya lekh_
_sadguru lekh mitaiya, tab paya nam alekh ||39||_
(O Jivan, what is written cannot be erased, whatever account has been written; but when the Sadguru erased that written account, then we obtained the Name that cannot be grasped [alekh].)

Whatever account of karma the Creator (Vidhata) has written according to one's deeds cannot be erased by anyone, but when the Sadguru erased that account of destiny, we then obtained the Name of God which cannot ordinarily be recognized. Adhyaruji too says—

_abhakta janpe karma karave, karma bhogavava deh dharave_
_sevak karma kashano hari hari_
(For one who is not a devotee, Hari makes him perform action and makes him take a body to undergo its fruit — but what action can attach to Your servant, O Hari, Hari!)

For a person who is not a devotee, God causes him to perform actions, and he must take a body to undergo their fruit. But how can action bind Your servant? A servant acts on his master's behalf and does as the master directs; therefore whatever good or bad deed the servant does, its fruit does not have to be undergone by the servant — no fault attaches to him. If there is profit or loss, the master bears it. In the same way, whatever God makes a devotee do, the bondage of that action does not attach to the devotee, whether it be good or bad. So then how is one to become free from this current of action?

Adhyaruji Maharaj gives the answer to this too: undergo the old actions, and give up — or disregard — new ones, and he has shown the entire process for how this should be done, because the current of karma is deep and profound. Can one not obtain release from it? This process is worth knowing. First, one offers every action to Krishna (Krishnarpan) — do not take its responsibility upon yourself. In this way no new action will attach. The second point is that remembrance of the Name should never be given up; one should always keep remembering the "Name" that the Sadguru has given. Through this simple process, freedom from action is easily attained.

Now comes the most important matter: having understood all these points, how should true devotion to Vishnu be practised, and what is to be understood of it? Jivanji Maharaj has explained the prevalent devotion to Vishnu under three heads, which we have already seen in the previous chapter: 1. Pushtimargi 2. Maryada-margi 3. Pravah-margi — these divisions were laid down by Vallabhacharya. There are four traditions (sampradayas) prevalent for the worship of Vishnu, namely: 1. Vishnu Acharya 2. Ramanujacharya 3. Madhvacharya 4. Vallabhacharya. Thus these four Acharyas widely propagated Vaishnava devotion throughout India.

Even so, all four Acharyas were unable to agree with one another on matters of doctrine. For this reason, at the time of the founding of Patan Vadi, Padmanabh did not give these four traditions a place within the circumambulation path (parikrama) of the Vadi. Even today, in memory of these same four differing traditions, their clay plots (kyara) lie outside the main precinct of the Vadi. Only those who hold one common view, or are in agreement, are given entry into Padmavadi. It is for this very reason that Jivanji Maharaj, without giving room to disputation, has charted his own separate path. And from the very beginning Jivanji Maharaj has described us as being beyond the three gunas (qualities); in the same way he has given us a unique Vaishnava-hood that transcends these three paths, and along with this he has also given us a sign by which to recognise true Vaishnavas. Jivanji Maharaj says that the Pravah Marg is the true Vaishnava path, and its testimony (identification) has been supplied by Kabirji—

_kabir tirath kari kari jag mua, jude pani nahay_
_ram ram pokarate, jam ghasete jay ||1||_
_kabir pahan kera putala, kab sarja kartar_
_e bharuse je rahe, so buda kalidhar ||2||_
_kabir hambhi pathar pujate, jab hote ranke rojh_
_pedeme sadguru mila, tab dara shirka bojh ||3||_
_kabir duniya chali dehare, shish namavan jay_
_hirde mahi hari base, tu tahi chit lay ||4||_
_kabir pahanku kahe pujiye, janma na de e ja bap_
_andhe lok asha mukhi, vo hi khove aap ||5||_
_patthar puje hari mile, to mai jai puju pahad_
_shaligramse chakki bhali, je pis khay sansar ||6||_
_kabir kajal keri kothari, masi ke kiya kapat_
_pahan boi prithvi, pandit padi vat ||7||_
_deval ghantaol bajiya, pani aur pashan_
_pandit shikari jivana, mare karmake ban ||8||_
_jaha jaha pandit pav dhare, taha taha jamka vas_
_sant pav dhare jivana, taha sitapati avinash ||9||_
_bhat bhalera dekhiye, sakutke sardar_
_karma gohade jivana, ghalyo sab sansar ||10||_
(Kabir says: going on pilgrimage after pilgrimage the world has died, bathing in cold river water and crying out "Ram, Ram" — yet Yama still drags them away. Kabir says: idols are made of stone — when did the Creator ever fashion them so? Whoever rests his trust in them drowns in the dark river of the world. Kabir says: I too used to worship stones, back when I was as foolish as the wild deer of the forest; but on the path I met the true Guru, who then removed the burden from my head. Kabir says: the world goes to bow its head at temples, but Hari dwells within the heart — fix your mind there. Kabir says: why should stone be worshipped? It cannot give birth to you, that Father alone does. Blind people are hungry for hope, and thereby lose their very self. If God could be met by worshipping stone, I would go and worship a whole mountain; better than the Shaligram stone is a grinding-stone, which grinds grain that feeds the world. Kabir says: they keep the Divine shut up as if in a room blackened with lamp-soot, sealed with the doors of ink; they have sown stone across the earth, and the pandits have laid down this false path. Bells and gongs sound in the temples, amid water and stone; the pandit is a hunter, O Jivan, who shoots the arrows of ritual action. Wherever the pandit sets foot, there dwells Yama; but wherever the saint sets foot, O Jivan, there dwells the imperishable Lord of Sita. The tale-tellers may seem fine to look at, but they are the chiefs of the faithless; they have entangled the whole world, O Jivan, in the noose of ritual action.)

At the outset of this chapter, Jivanji Maharaj has, through the sakhis of Kabirji, shown what obstructs the essence of devotion and what its distorted form looks like, because the great sage Shandilya says—

"sa paranuraktirishvare" — supreme love (para-anurakti) for the Divine is itself devotion. That is, devotees are to fix their mind, their attachment (anuraga), on the essence of the Supreme Brahman alone, and not on outward observance and external ritual, because if this is done then the mind constantly wavers away from the Supreme Lord (Parameshvar) and becomes centred on outer conduct and thought, whereby the essence of devotion is disturbed, and with time devotion becomes secondary while outward observance takes on the form of the main thing. Indeed, this very practice has today taken root everywhere. This is precisely why Kabirji and open-minded saints like him have had to say that going on pilgrimage and then bathing there in the cold (jude) water of a river has become the ordinary habit of the common person. Kabirji says that in this way, chanting "Ram, Ram" while going on pilgrimages, lakhs of people have died, yet no one has attained deliverance.

Even if people bathe at pilgrimage sites calling out "Ram, Ram," without purity of feeling or conduct their sin does not depart — so he says—

_ram ram sabkoi kahe, thag thakur aur chor_
_bina prem rijhe nahi, ruda nand kishor_
(Everyone says "Ram, Ram" — the swindler, the lord, and the thief alike — but without love that lovely son of Nanda is not pleased.)

Everyone who walks about says "Ram Ram," whether a wealthy man or a thief; but this Name of Ram cannot be taken except with true love, and God does not become pleased with such deceivers.

But the way Kabirji himself takes the name of Ram is of quite another kind altogether—

_ram nam sab kahat hai, so to nam amir_
_ajar amar ek nam hai, vaku jape kabir_
(Everyone says the name of Ram, but that is merely the worldly, famous name; there is one imperishable, undying Name, and it is that Name which Kabir chants.)

Everyone says they take the name of Ram, but that name they mean is the well-known, famous name of King Ram; but Kabir takes that Name of Ram which is imperishable — that is the Name Kabir chants, meaning that Kabir worships Ram with a truly sincere heart. He does not, like everyone else, merely say "Ram Ram" emptily; therefore the Name of Ram that Kabir chants is the one filled with supreme, loving devotion.

Furthermore, "pahan kera putala" means idols made of stone — when did the Supreme Being ever make these? There is no end to those who worship these very stones, believing them to be God. (Every ancient temple's image, it is said, manifested itself.) And such blindly faithful people finally fall into the mouth of death itself. —2.

(In Ratnasar, Part 4, page 295, it is written: there is no statement in the Vedas about the worship of the image. Just as there is not a single mantra in the Vedas on the subject of invocation, installation of life-breath, and so forth for a stone image, so too there is not even this much of a statement—

_pashanadi murti rachayitva mandireshu samsthapya gandhabhirarchayet_
(having fashioned a stone image and installed it in a temple, one should worship it with sandal-paste and rice grains)

— that is, there is not the slightest such statement in the Vedas that one should fashion a stone image, install it in a temple, and worship it with sandal paste, unbroken rice, and so on.

In the Dasbodh, dashak of the chhand, sixth samas, it is said: Shri Krishna, king of all the wise, says — "murkhasya pratimapuja" — image-worship is for fools.)

In the Padma Purana it is said—

_uttama sahajavastha madhyama dhyana dharana_
_adhama tirthavastha murtipuja'dhamadhamah_
(The natural, spontaneous state is the highest; meditation and concentration are the middling state; the state of dependence on pilgrimage is the lowest; and image-worship is the lowest of the low.)

The natural state is the highest state, meditation and concentration are the middling state, but the state of pilgrimage is the lowest state, and moreover image-worship is the lowest of the low states.

_sajive nirjivane ghadyo, nam dharyo dev_
_hetho thaine paye lage, ek phuti ke bev_
(A living man carved a lifeless thing and gave it the name of God; then bending low he falls at its feet — has one of your eyes gone blind, or both?)

A living human being fashioned a lifeless thing and gave it the name of a deity; then, bending down, he falls at its feet — has one of your eyes gone blind, or are both blind, that you cannot see this is merely a carved image?

Asavari (raga):

_duniya jhamar jhol valudhi, rajaram bhagati nahi sujhi ||tek||_
_tel bakala bhairav mage, kandh ajako kate_
_puja to bhopo (bhuvo) le gayo, pathar kutta chate ||1||_
_mathe balati mele angithi, math devike chali_
_khanpan sab taj kar baithi, narak kundale dhali ||2||_
_khetarpalpe beta mage, aja sutke sate_
_apano put jivayo chahe, put piyaro kate ||3||_
_sasara jeth dekhata dode, nara bhajave bhaje_
_harijan dekhi ghunghat tane, pranam karati laje ||4||_
_koi devika koi devka, koi chamandaka hosi_
_gunakake ghar beta jaya, pita konasu kahesi ||5||_
_atham karai ahori puje, dos daman bandhe_
_hansi hosi sinhan vahan, ko gadhe ko gadhe ||6||_
_vijhasanko pehero jhalaro, murakh raat jagai_
_kal padyo tab bechi khayo, kaha gai sukalai ||7||_
_atham chaudas kare lapasi, haran hi bhog lagave_
_raat jagave dhola maru, sonal vijha gave ||8||_
_hati ekal bhai anekki, veshya bahu bharathari_
_kahat kabir kaun sang chalegi, bahot purushki nari ||9||_
(In the Asavari raga: the people of the world hang uselessly in a swing of pomp and show — devotion to Rajaram never even occurs to them. Bhairav demands oil and gram, and a goat's neck is cut for him; the offering made to him is carried off by the shaman, and dogs lick the blood-stained stone. Women go to the goddess's shrine carrying a burning brazier on their heads, giving up all food and drink, sitting there with a hell of flesh beside them. They ask Kshetrapal for a son in exchange for the sacrifice of a goat — wishing to save their own dear son's life, they cut down the goat's own beloved kid. In the presence of father-in-law and brother-in-law they rush off to such places, hiding their face behind a veil, yet feel shy to bow before true devotees of Hari. Among those who practise this devotion she has set going, some will worship a goddess, some a god, some Chamunda; when a courtesan's son is born, whom can he even call father? She keeps the eighth-day fast and worships the smallpox goddess, and ties charm-threads against possession and misfortune — but it becomes a laughing matter, for one goddess's mount is a donkey, another's a lion or bull. Wearing a fringed skirt, the fool keeps vigil all night; but when calamity strikes she sells it all and eats — where then has all your fine skill gone? On the eighth and fourteenth days she cooks sweet lapsi and offers it to these deities, and stays awake all night singing worldly songs. She who was devoted to one alone has become devoted to many, like a courtesan with many husbands; Kabir says: with which one, then, will she go in the end, she who is wife to so many men?)

The people of the world remain caught up, dangling in a meaningless, worthless swing — that is, they remain occupied in wandering about — but devotion to Rajaram does not occur to them. Bhairav demands oil and grains of gram, and they offer him a goat by cutting its neck. The offering made to Bhairav is carried off by the shaman (bhuvo); and the blood that clings to Bhairav's stone is licked by dogs. Women go to the goddess's shrine carrying a burning brazier upon their heads; giving up all food and drink there, they sit as though placing hell itself, in the form of flesh, beside them. They ask Kshetrapal, the guardian deity of the field, for the gift of a son in exchange for the sacrifice of a goat. They wish to save the life of their own dear son, yet they cut down and kill the dear kid of a goat. In the presence of her father-in-law or brother-in-law, she rushes off swiftly to such a place; she covers her face with a veil out of modesty before them, yet feels ashamed to bow in respect when she sees devotees of Hari. Thus, among those who practise the impure devotion she has set going, causing pure devotion to be broken, and before whom devotees feel embarrassed even to greet with respect — some among these will turn out to be worshippers of one goddess, some of one god, and some of Chamunda. So if a courtesan's house has a son born to it, whom can he call his father? She keeps the eighth-day fast, worships the smallpox goddess, and to ward off obstruction and possession and their attendant troubles she ties charm-threads — and this becomes a laughable disgrace, because one such goddess's mount is a donkey while another's is a bull or lion. Furthermore, she wears a garment that flaps about at its hem; and fools have spent the whole night in loud vigil for her worship, and when misfortune actually struck, they abandoned it all and let it go — where then did all your fine skills go? On the eighth and fourteenth days and other such occasions, she prepares sweet lapsi and offers this to these goddesses, and thus she awakens her infatuated devotees and sings beautiful, sensuous songs. She was once the devoted worshipper of only one Husband, the Supreme Lord, but now has become the worshipper of many — she has become a courtesan with many husbands; so then, in the end, with which one of her many husbands will she burn? Therefore Kabir resolved—

_ab mai jana he mere bhai, bhuli duniya kal gher jai |tek|_
_nahi ma puju devadevi, nahi me pushp chadhavu_
_nahi me singhasan murati dharu, nahi me ghant bajavu ||1||_
_jo e murati jutha jame, khara mora kahi jane_
_pani mag pie apane mukh hase, to mera man man ||2||_
_jo e murat mukhse bole, to kar jodi shish namavu_
_char paisa le sonar ghar javu, me bi ek gadhau ||3||_
_tank tank kar gadhi re sonare, ber ber tapae_
_e muratke bharuse rahave, to agale janamki kamai ||4||_
_gyan kare hardai nache te, grahame rahe udasi_
_satanam the duna jage, kahe kabir avinashi ||5||_
(Now, my brother, I have understood: the deluded world goes into the clutches of death. Now I will worship no god or goddess, nor offer flowers to any; I will not install any idol on a throne, nor ring any temple bell. If this idol could know stale, impure food and salty water for what it is, if it could ask for water and drink it, and smile with its own mouth — then my mind would believe. If this idol could speak with its own mouth, I would fold my hands and bow my head to it; I would take my four coins — my little wealth — and go to a goldsmith's house, and have one cast for myself too. Beaten and beaten into shape, heated again and again by the goldsmith — if one could rely upon such an image, it would be the fruit of merit earned in a former birth! One who takes up true knowledge dances with joy in the heart, and remains detached even while living in the household; through the True Name he awakens doubly, says Kabir, the Name which is imperishable.)

O my brother, now I have realised that the whole world, having lost its way, is heading into the house of death. Now I shall no longer worship any god or goddess nor offer them flowers. I shall not enshrine any idol upon a throne nor ring any temple bell. If this idol could know that it has become stale, impure, or salty water, and if it could ask for water and drink it, or laugh with its mouth, then indeed I would come to believe. If that idol could speak with its mouth, I would bow my head to it; moreover, whatever four or five paise — that is, whatever wealth — I possess, I would take that money to a goldsmith and have an idol cast for myself as well. If the goldsmith, by hammering it again and again and heating it repeatedly, has fashioned it, then to be able to rely on such an image would be reckoned the fruit of merit from a past birth. Those who grasp true knowledge and remain joyful and content at heart, remaining equally detached in happiness and sorrow, experience double happiness through the Name of God — so speaks the soul of the devotee Kabir.

Kabirji says that just as "I too used to worship stones" — the wild deer of the forest are of no use to human beings at all, and moreover they cause damage to the standing crops of farmers; had I been as devoid of intelligence as they, I too would have worshipped stone. In the same way, such stone deities are useless. On this path of devotion, when I — that is, this body of mine — found the true Sadguru, he freed me from the burden upon my head, that is, from the act of worshipping various stones. —3.

O foolish one! Every day the people of this world get up in the morning and go to worship stones in temples; there they go and bow head upon head. But you are unable to recognise that Hari dwells within this very body, within the heart; fix your mind there — upon that inner being of yours where Hari dwells. —4.

Why should stone be worshipped, when it is not living and cannot give birth? Yet people call it their Supreme Father, the Lord! Because blind people are hungry for hope, for gain, they thus waste their own lives wherever it pleases them. —5.

_baitha so bole nahi, ubha kahe na av_
_suta so jage nahi, kisku lagu pay_
(Seated, it does not speak; standing, it does not say "come"; lying down, it does not wake — then to whom shall I bow my feet?)

The idol that is seated does not speak; the idol that stands does not say "come"; the idol that lies asleep does not wake — then at whose feet shall I bow?

If one could obtain the Supreme Brahman by worshipping stones, then I, Kabirji, would be ready to go and worship an entire mountain; but that is not how it happens. Alas, people worship a stone called Shaligram, taking it to be Vishnu and Shiva, but that is of no use at all, because the millstone used for grinding grain is more useful than the Shaligram; through it the worldly soul grinds grain daily and eats bread, whereas the stones of temples are of no use whatsoever. —6.

In a dark chamber of ignorance and nescience, people have imprisoned God and set out to search for Hari in a temple built of four walls. So-called pious men and pandits have set up this strange and false path. The whole world in this way has lost its way, running after stones. —7.

In books written with black ink, binding these teachings into fixed form and spreading them across the earth, and by building temples of stone across the earth, sowing the seed of scripture in people's minds, the pandits have laid down a set custom for people to follow accordingly.

After this utterance of Kabirji, Jivanji Maharaj says that bells are rung in temples, and the stone idol is bathed and anointed with water and so forth just as one would treat a living human being, and all manner of ceremonial dealing is carried out with it as though it were alive; but the eyes of the pandits and priests who perform this worship are fixed not on devotion but on the donations of the assembled devotees. Thus they are like hunters, and they draw us into the net of ritual action. —8.

Sadguru Jivanji Maharaj, on the basis of the Bijak, Shabda 11, has called the pandit a hunter.

Shabda 11:

_santo pande nipun kasai_
_bakara mari bhainsa par ghave, dilme dard na ai ||tek||_
_kari asnan tilak dai baithe, bidhise devi pujai_
_atamram palakme binashe, rudhir ki nadi bahai ||1||_
_ati punit unche kul kahiye, sabha mahi adhikai_
_inhate diksha sab koi mange, hansi ave mohi bhai ||2||_
_pap katanko katha sunave, karma karave nicha_
_ham to dou paraspar dekha, yam laye hai dhokha ||3||_
_gay badhe te turuk kahiye, inhate vai kya chhote_
_kahihi kabir suno ho santo, kali me brahman khote ||4||_
(O saints, the pandit is a skilled butcher: he kills goats and strikes down buffaloes, and feels not the least pain of it in his heart. After bathing, he sits down having applied his tilak, and worships the goddess with proper ritual; in a moment he destroys the indwelling soul and makes a river of blood flow. Yet these are called of most holy, high lineage, and are given the highest place in assemblies; everyone begs initiation from them — it makes me, brother, want to laugh. They recite tales meant to remove sin, yet cause the lowest deeds to be done; I have watched the two of them side by side — Yama has fashioned them as one deception. He who kills a cow is called a Turk — how are these Brahmins any less than him? Kabir says: listen, O saints, in the Kali Yuga the Brahmins have become corrupted.)

O saints, the pandit is a cunning butcher, because he rushes to kill goats and buffaloes and feels not the slightest pain in his heart at slaughtering creatures small or great. Having bathed, he sits down after applying his tilak. He performs and has others perform the worship of the goddess by tantric ritual. Then, after killing an animal, he offers it as sacrifice to the goddess. In doing so he kills, in an instant, the very indwelling Self within that creature, and makes a river of blood flow. These people bearing the name of "Pandey" commit such violent, vile deeds, and yet call themselves the most exalted, of the highest and purest lineage; and in assemblies and gatherings they are praised. People take guru-diksha, the initiation mantra, from these very gurus — seeing this whole tradition of the ignorant makes me want to laugh, and I grow troubled. These priests named Pandey recite religious discourses to free their patrons from sin, while themselves causing the base act of violence to be committed. I have watched both Hindu and Turk (Muslim) alike commit the killing of living beings; Yama has fashioned instruments to lead both of them to hell. One who kills a cow is called a Turk; but Brahmins who kill goats and buffaloes are no less sinful than him — both are equally sinful. In the Kali Yuga, both the Brahmins and the Muslims who cause the killing of living beings are sinners. In the Hindi Collection (H. Li. Granth) No. 8, page 62, in the Asavari raga, Kabir says—

_ape betha loh nav par, orakun ehi dadhai_
_kahat kabir kashithe kadho, brahman jo hai kasai_
(He himself sits on an iron boat, urging others to place this very confidence in it; Kabir says: throw out of Kashi that Brahmin who is a butcher.)

_rakshasah kalimashritya jayate brahmayonishu_
(In the Kali Yuga, demons will take birth in the wombs of Brahmins.)

That is, when the Kali Yuga arrives, demons will be born upon this earth in the form of Brahmins. "If we were asked to give the definition of a devotee in a single word, we would place before it the word 'lokbahya' [beyond ordinary worldly convention]. In this single word alone the entire definition of the devotee's life, of the traveller on the sacred path of devotion, is expressed. All the deeds of devotees are wondrous indeed; they have no concern for what people think." — Prabhudutt Brahmachari, Shri Chaitanya Mahaprabhu, page 534.

Wherever the pandits go — that is, wherever pandits enter, or whatever matter they meddle in — there they look only to their own self-interest; therefore for such people only exploitation remains, that is, death! But wherever the feet of a saint fall, there the Supreme Brahman comes to dwell. —9.

The bards and minstrels who entertain people while also instructing them through tales and stories, though these tale-telling bhats or Brahmins may appear innocent on the surface, are in truth the very chiefs of the faithless (sakut). Under their innocent-sounding words, the world is unknowingly led astray. Thus they are well capable of leading society down the wrong path.

_kabir panditki katha, jaisi chorank nav_
_sunkar baithe andhala, bhave taha le jay_
(Kabir says: the discourse of the pandit is like the boat of thieves — the blind sit and listen to it, and it takes them wherever it pleases.)

The discourses of Brahmins are like the boat of thieves. Those ignorant ones who are lured in by listening to such discourses are taken by the Brahmins wherever they please, and are robbed after being set down there.

_ishta bina bhajan kesu, jyu khevat bin nav_
_moji pari parabhayome, jit bhave tit jay_
(Without one's chosen deity, worship of another is like a boat without a boatman — carried by the current wherever it happens to go, into difficulty.)

Moji Bhagat says: how can one be called a devotee who, without an Ishtadev, one's own chosen deity, worships another deity instead? It is like a boat without a boatman, which, once cast adrift in the current, goes wherever it happens to go.

_kabir brahman guru jagatka, santanka guru nahi_
_lot potke dubiya, charo vedo mahi_
(Kabir says: the Brahmin is guru to the world, but he is no guru to the saints; rolling about, they drown, the four Vedas notwithstanding.)

The Veda-reciting, ritualistic Brahmins are gurus who lead worldly people, entangled in the wheel of the material world, along the path of ritual action; but saints are free from hope of illusory fruit, and therefore these Brahmins are not their gurus. So, entangled in the four Vedas, floundering and struggling, they — the people of the world as well as the Brahmins — sink lower and lower, drowning again and again in the net of illusion (maya).

This teaching above has been spoken by Sadguru Kabirji and Jivanji Maharaj, and the Purana bears witness to this very teaching. Shloka:

_tvam gantarah prapadyante vina bhaktya na chantimam_
_shastrani vedamarganam deva vishnorbahirmukhah ||44||_
(Those who go toward You cannot attain that ultimate goal without devotion; the gods who are turned away from Vishnu, as well as the paths of the Vedas and the scriptures, cannot attain You either.)

Without devotion, people travelling toward that supreme abode which is You cannot attain You. The gods who are turned away from Vishnu, and the path of the Vedas and the scriptures, cannot attain You.

Now the commentary (tika): Mahadev spoke, saying, "O beloved! That state which is of the nature of bliss, which is the supreme Vishnu — that supreme Vishnu is our very protector." Agradas likewise says—

_trata to tin lokme, jit dekho tit soi_
_santanka veri koi nahi, hoi to brahman hoi_
(Our protector, wherever you look in all three worlds, is that very one; the saints have no enemy at all — if they have any, it is only the Brahmin.)

Agradas says: in all three worlds, wherever we look, it is that same protector who is present to save us, the saints and devotees; but if the saints have any enemy at all in this world, it is only the Brahmin.

_nalam dvijatvam devatvam rishitvam vasuratmajah_
_prananatha mukundasya na vrittam na bahujnata_
_na danam na tapo nejya na shaucham na vratani cha_
_priyate'amalaya bhaktya harliranyad vidambana_
(Bhagavata, Skandha 7, Adhyaya 7 — O son of the demon! Brahminhood, godhood, or sagehood, good conduct, vast learning, charity, austerity, sacrifice, purity, or great vows — none of these are able to please Mukunda, the Lord of life; He is pleased only by pure, desireless devotion — all else is mere pretence.)

Brahminhood, godhood, or the state of a sage, good conduct, deep scriptural learning, and also charity, austerity, sacrifice, physical and mental purity, and even great vows — none of these are capable of pleasing God. God is pleased only by pure, desireless (nishkam) devotion. Everything else is mere theatrical show.

_brahmanke man bhakti na ave, bhule ap sabani samujhave_
_aurani thagi-thagi apun thagave, apun sove sabani jagave_
_ved-puran bechi dhan lyave, satya taji hatyadi milave_
_hari haridas na dekhyau bhave, bhuta, pitar, devata pujave_
_apun narak pari kulahi bulave, vyas bhakti binu ko gati pavau_
(233; Bhaktakavi Vyas, page 245 — Devotion never enters the Brahmin's mind — himself astray, he goes about instructing everyone else. Cheating others again and again, he ends up cheating himself; asleep himself, he wakes everyone else. Selling the Vedas and Puranas, he makes his money; abandoning truth, he takes up violence and the like. He has no love for seeing Hari or Hari's devotees, yet he makes people worship ghosts, ancestors, and lesser deities. He drags his own family down into hell with himself — says Vyas, without devotion who can attain true liberation?)

The thought of devotion to Vishnu never even enters the mind of Brahmins; they themselves are lost in the worship of Anadev, other deities, yet they instruct everyone else to practise devotion to Vishnu and to Anadev alike. Cheating others again and again, they end up cheating themselves, thereby becoming bound for hell. They themselves practise neither devotion to Vishnu nor any other true devotion, yet they warn everyone else to do so. They sell the Vedas and Puranas and earn money by it, and abandoning the true they pursue the false; they have no love at all for the sight of God or of God's devotees, and instead make people worship ghosts, ancestral spirits, and lesser deities. Thus they themselves fall into hell along with their whole lineage. And how can one attain any good state at all, without devotion?

The revered Yadunath Maharaj has written in Litiyu No. 74, page 1, that no living being can remain in this world without practising some form of devotion — this is beyond dispute. It is said in the Gita: _na hi kashchitkshanamapi jatu tishthatyakarmakrit_ (Chapter 3, verse 5) — no person can ever remain even for an instant without performing action. In the same way, everyone practises some devotion, but only devotion to the Supremely Merciful One is truly glorious; anything else is merely a burden, like forced labour —

therefore it is most beneficial to worship the Supreme Lord of all through this human body. Hence, even the ascetics who renounce all attachment, the sages who keep perpetual silence, and gods such as Narada, Sanaka, Sanandana and the rest, who without devotion still fear birth and death — the recurring cycle of birth and death and rebirth, that is, the fear of death — that fear does not remain if one practises devotion. Therefore it is essential that anyone who takes a human body must certainly practise devotion. The reason is that the wisdom to practise devotion is not even possessed by the gods and great sages — that is, by Indra and the like — because to practise devotion, it is first necessary to take refuge (sharanagati); refuge alone is the key to victory. The Supremely Merciful One, along with His compassion, is the giver of the imperishable state; Dhruva and Prahlad stand as the very examples, the proof, of that imperishable state and of firm resolve — therefore it is necessary to take refuge in the Lord of all. For taking refuge, do not forget Vibhishan.

This has been described as the dharma of the Treta Yuga, and called the Pravah-Margi Vaishnava dharma. The devotion to Vishnu practised in the Satya, Treta, and Dvapar Yugas has been discussed here; that path of devotion has been called the Pravah Marg. Now let us speak of the glory of the Pushti Marg: Rudra spoke to Parvati, describing the dharma of the Dvapar Yuga. The Pushti Marg is one of devotion to Krishna, and for this reason this path has been placed within the dharma of the Dvapar Yuga. Shloka:

_navaishnavaya datavyam vikalpaya hatatmane_
_bhaktishraddhavihinaya vishnunamadruhe na cha ||45||_
(This should not be given to one who is not a Vaishnava, who is caught in doubt and vacillation, who is spiritually ruined, who is devoid of devotion and faith, or who bears hostility toward the Name of Vishnu.)

This — the Ram Name — should not be given to one who is not a Vaishnava, who is caught up in doubt and vacillation, who is spiritually ruined, who is devoid of devotion and faith, and who bears enmity toward the Name of Vishnu. It has been said in shloka 45 —

_bhakti shraddhavihinaya_ — that is, to one who is devoid of devotion and faith, who has no faith for devotion, the Ram Name should not be given; regarding this it has been said —

_ashraddhane vimukhe'pyashrunvanti yashchopadeshah shivanamaparadhah_
(To teach the divine name to those who are faithless, turned away, and unwilling to listen — that itself is an offence against the sacred Name.)

Those who are faithless and turned away — that is, who direct their senses toward worldly objects — if the teaching of God is spoken to such people, it becomes an offence against the divine Name.

Kabirji made efforts to teach people devotion to God; even after being explained to once, twice, three times, when such shakta-worshipping, faithless people did not accept it, Kabirji, growing weary, called such people "sakut" (the faithless), and gave the injunction not to keep company with them, because upon persons of such varied and contrary nature no good effect is produced — rather, the opposite effect results, and they turn against us instead.

_kabir kalika ramjan, mata jaisa dhing_
_keval gyan dradhavate, sahama mande sing_
(Kabir says: in the Kali Yuga, some so-called devotees of Ram are like a mad, intoxicated animal; when one tries firmly to instill true knowledge in them, they lower their horns to charge.)

Kabirji says that in the Kali Yuga there are people, like mourners at a cremation ground, who behave like an intoxicated bull; when one goes to impress the true teaching upon them, they instead pick a quarrel with us.

_khalah sakriyamanopi dadati kalaham satam_
_dugdha dyotopi kim yati vayasah kalahamsatam_
(Even when good is done to him, the wicked man repays the virtuous with strife; even if bathed in milk, does a crow ever become a swan?)

Even if you do good to a wicked man, he will still do evil to the virtuous. Even if you bathe a crow in milk, it will never become a swan.

Vasant (raga):

_harirasa ajar mahara vahala, jirave virala koi_
_mand agni mishthanna na jirave, vaman kare taha soi_
_paro bhogave te bhogi kahiye, man bhogave te jogi_
_jaha lagi man paro nahi bhogave, taha lagi e bhayrogi ||1||_
_gay sikhe ne mota bole, em mota nav thaiye_
_moti dasha mota anubhav vina, parangat nav thaiye ||2||_
_megh vrishti kare nirantar, jal jai thambhe khame_
_sathu solu sovarnanu patra, tame sinhaninu dudh jame ||3||_
_svant tana meh saghale vutha, sip tharya te moti_
_kone kadhya kashta karine, pahere te panoti ||4||_
_shura je ranthi pachha na bhage, pura padma sahamai_
_sati bhando sanche nahi koi, pith na puthe palai ||5||_
_pandit te je sada sam drashti, vaid te je arogi_
_shubh ashubh jehane nahi sambhave, so nar sudha jogi ||6||_
_man pasarya hoy te pachha sankeli, niralamb thai rahiye_
_kahe kabir prem jal parasata, sada anand sukh paiye ||7||_
(The rasa of devotion to Hari is imperishable, my dear one, but only a rare few can digest it; one of weak digestion cannot digest sweets, and if he eats them he vomits at once. He who can digest raw mercury is the true "enjoyer"; he whose mind does not become attached to enjoyment is the true "yogi." So long as the mind has not, of its own accord, digested and conquered the mercury of illusion, one remains diseased with worldly desire. One who merely learns to sing like a cow and calls himself great does not thereby become great; without deep experience of the great state, one does not become perfect. The cloud rains ceaselessly, yet that water only collects and stops in a pit; only in a vessel of sixteen-anna pure gold can the milk of a lioness be kept without spoiling. When the rain of the Svati star falls, all showers fall alike, but only in an oyster-shell does it become a pearl; only a fortunate soul, after great labour, can pull that pearl out of the sea and wear it. The brave warrior does not flee from the battlefield, but faces it with full strength; the chaste woman never harbours another man in truth, and never turns her back to flee. The true pandit is one who always looks upon all with equal vision, and the true physician is the one who himself remains free of disease. He for whom good and bad fortune no longer arise is the true, nectar-drinking yogi. If the mind has strayed outward, one should draw it back inward again, and remain independent of all external support; Kabir says, by touching the water of divine love, one attains everlasting bliss and joy.)

Beloved ones, the rasa (essence) of devotion to Hari is such that it never spoils, yet only a rare few are able to digest it. Those of weak digestive power cannot digest sweets — if they eat them, they immediately vomit. Those who have such a strong digestive fire that they can digest even raw mercury, and who are able likewise to digest illusion (maya), are the true "bhogis," enjoyers; in the same way, those whose mind does not attach itself to maya are called "yogis." So long as the mind has not, through its own will, released and thus digested the mercury-like maya, such people remain afflicted with the disease of worldly desire. Those who, after learning to sing beautifully and gaining some knowledge, declare themselves to have become great, do not thereby become truly great; without deep, profound experience they fall into great calamity, and one who is incomplete cannot become a perfect scholar. Even if rain falls continuously, that water only collects and stays in a hollow; only in a vessel of sixteen-anna pure gold can the milk of a lioness be kept — in any other vessel it curdles and spoils.

When the water of the Svati constellation falls and lands in an oyster shell, it becomes a pearl; and that pearl is brought up from the sea by some diver who endures great hardship to fetch it, and whoever wears it must be a person of great merit. One who does not flee from the battlefield is called a hero; he charges forward with full strength and power to face the enemy. A chaste woman (sati) never keeps company with another man, and in remaining true to her chastity she never turns her back and runs away. The true pandit is one who always looks with an equal eye upon all, and the true physician is one who himself remains free of disease. Only those men in whom no distinction of good fortune and bad fortune arises are the truly wise yogis. If the mind has wandered off into sensual desire, it should be drawn back from there, and one should remain independent, without relying upon anything else. Kabir says: experiencing thus the water of loving devotion, may we always attain the bliss of joy.

Ignorant, worldly people are one thing, but even great scholars regard Anadev and Ishtadev — other deities — as equal to Vasudev, the Supreme Lord — and this is worse still, for such scholars have left nothing undone in reducing Vasudev to the level of an ordinary human being. Not only this, but it is a matter of great regret that even the Vaishnava Acharyas, who insist on purity of conduct, lend great support to such a view. That regrettable attitude toward Ram and Krishna is this: that at the time of the birth of Ram and Krishna, a period of ritual impurity (sutak) is observed, and so people delay eating their meal after the birth of Ram and Krishna, as if it were an ordinary human birth involving pollution. In this way, they regard Ram and Krishna, who are the mighty Supreme Purushottam themselves, as being lower even than ordinary gods, as mere humans. Therefore devotion which behaves in this manner toward God is faulty, and those who hold such faulty devotion fall into the category of the faithless (sakut).

Rudra says to Parvati: O beloved! Those who are non-Vaishnava (sakut), devoid of devotion and faith, who regard Anadev as equal to Vasudev — such ignorant people should not be given the Ram Name.

Kabirji says—

_kabir sakutkun na sunaiye, gun gan aur git_
_tulsi manjar todke, kyu chadhaiye masit ||1||_
_ramabhaktima jivana, vali anadev upas_
_khir khanekihush hai, pan bhele dudh aur chhas ||2||_
_anadev barabar jivana, je samare sitaram_
_mugatphal ve det he, nahi charan kamal vishram ||3||_
_sitapati taj jivana, dhyan dhare akash_
_pragat godko chhandke, kare garbhaki ash ||4||_
_sitapati taj jivana, rahyo brahmasu lag_
_rui mandirme peth kar, dvare lagai ag ||5||_
(Kabir says: do not sing praises and songs of Hari to the faithless — plucking tulsi buds and offering them at a mosque, what purpose does that serve? O Jivan, in devotion to Ram, worship also of Anadev — it is as if one desires to eat kheer, yet mixes buttermilk into the milk. O Jivan, whoever ranks Anadev equal to Ram and yet remembers Sitaram — such worship grants only the four lesser liberations, not rest at those lotus feet. O Jivan, forsaking the Lord of Sita, some meditate gazing at the sky — it is like a mother, holding her manifest child already in her lap, instead longing for a child still in the womb. O Jivan, forsaking the Lord of Sita, remaining attached to abstract Brahman alone — it is like entering a house made of cotton and lighting a fire at its very door.)

That is, Kabirji says that to those who are "sakut," faithless, one should not recite the qualities or hymns of Shri Hari Bhagwan, or sing devotional songs, because they are not entitled to it. There is no purpose in plucking tulsi leaves and offering them at a mosque — it would only bring disrespect upon us. In the same way, there is no purpose in showing or reciting the Name of God to the faithless — they will only show disrespect to God. —1.

_mul dvare edi dai, pavan valove akash_
_sitapati bin jivana, svarg narak mahi vas ||6||_
_anahad shabda jaha unmuni, ravi shashi donu mel_
_ramnam bin jivana, jamsu karvo kel ||7||_
_ashtadal kamal je koi jape, koi dhyan dhare akash_
_bhaj sitapati jivana, lakshmi charan nivas ||8||_
(Placing the heel at the base and churning the sky with the breath — O Jivan, without the Lord of Sita, one dwells only between heaven and hell. Where the unstruck sound arises in the state beyond mind, where sun and moon are merged as one — O Jivan, without the Name of Ram, one must play games with Yama. Whether one meditates repeating the eight-petalled lotus, or fixes contemplation on the sky — O Jivan, worship the Lord of Sita instead, at whose feet Lakshmi herself dwells.)

Jivanji Maharaj says that in devotion to Ram, worship of Anadev — other gods and goddesses — cannot stand together with it. For just as one may wish to eat kheer, but if buttermilk gets mixed into the milk meant for making that kheer, the kheer of that milk cannot be made — in the same way, in the devotion of true, unique Vaishnavism, no worship of Anadev can stand alongside it. Moreover, in devotion to Sitaram, worship of Anadev, of other gods and goddesses, cannot stand; the faithless are worshippers of Anadev, and therefore, just as milk curdles and spoils when mixed with something else, Ram-bhakti mixed with worship of Anadev likewise becomes useless. —2.

Sakhi 3 follows on from Sakhi 2. In Sakhi 2 it is said that if one who practises devotion to Ram also worships Anadev, then, just as milk curdles, the devotion to Ram, though practised, becomes corrupted. So in Sakhi 3 it is said that those who worship Anadev while also practising remembrance-devotion to Ram — such devotion to Ram becomes just like devotion to Anadev; therefore, though they are indeed practising devotion to Ram as well, they obtain only the fruit of the four lesser liberations, but they cannot attain the supreme state of dwelling at the lotus feet of God. Anadev must never be compared with Ram, because Ram cannot be compared with other deities — He is the Supreme, the highest God, the Supreme Brahman. He is omniscient, all-pervading, all-powerful. Therefore Ram and Anadev must not be worshipped as though they were equal; otherwise, by doing so, the worshipper does indeed reap the fruit of that devotion, but he cannot find rest at the feet of Shri Hari. —3.

Forsaking the Lord of Sita, many people seek the Supreme Brahman by meditating and searching for it in the sky. But this is like a pregnant woman whose first child is already playing in her lap, yet who neglects that child and instead remains absorbed in thoughts about the child still...
